subject: chemistry
question_text: Balance the following redox reaction by the ion-electron method (in acidic medium): Cr₂O₇²⁻(aq) + SO₂(g) → Cr³⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq).

verification.note: Chapter 5 (Stoichiometry) is sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack chemistry section (book pp.66-72), which prints the question, its star rank, the citation [March-09] and a model answer. Only ONE source book is held for chemistry — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only — so the two-book union check is PENDING a second chemistry source. This chapter has NO Long Answer section in the book, so no 8-mark form is invented. The 1+1+1+1 mark split is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. The final equation was independently re-checked: atoms Cr 2=2, S 3=3, O 13=13, H 2=2; charge 0 on each side.

steps.label: Identifying the two half reactions
lines: S in SO₂ is +4 → +6 in SO₄²⁻ : oxidation
Cr in Cr₂O₇²⁻ is +6 → +3 in Cr³⁺ : reduction
steps.why: Sulphur rises two units and each of the two chromium atoms falls three, which fixes the halves and later the multipliers 3 and 1.
common_mistakes: Mislabelling the halves. Dichromate is the oxidising agent, so it is itself reduced.
Computing Cr in Cr₂O₇²⁻ as +7 — the sum 2x − 14 = −2 gives +6.
steps.memory_tip: Write the oxidation numbers over the changing atoms in all four species before splitting the halves.
steps.margin_note: Both skeleton halves with the +4→+6 and +6→+3 changes earn this mark.

steps.label: Balanced oxidation half
lines: Balance O with H₂O, H with H⁺, charge with e⁻:
steps.why: Two waters supply the two extra oxygens and release all four hydrogens as H⁺ this time, since sulphate holds no hydrogen; the charge check fixes two electrons.
common_mistakes: Writing 3H⁺ from the HSO₄⁻ variant of this question. Sulphate keeps no hydrogen — all four leave.
Placing the electrons on the reactant side.
steps.memory_tip: SO₄²⁻ product: 4H⁺ out. HSO₄⁻ product: 3H⁺ out. Read which product the question gives.
steps.margin_note: Equation (1) with its charge check earns this mark.

steps.label: Balanced reduction half
steps.why: Both chromium atoms drop three units each, so the half consumes six electrons, confirmed by the charge check.
common_mistakes: Writing 3e⁻ for a single chromium and forgetting the ion carries two.
steps.memory_tip: Dichromate in acid: 14H⁺ in, 7H₂O out, 6e⁻ gained — the same stock line every time.
steps.margin_note: Equation (2) with its charge check earns this mark.

steps.label: Adding and the final equation
lines: Add (2) and cancel 12H⁺ and 6H₂O from both sides:
Check: Cr 2=2, S 3=3, O 13=13, H 2=2; charge 0 = 0
steps.why: Tripling the sulphur half matches six electrons; cancelling 12 of the 14 H⁺ and 6 of the 7 H₂O leaves 2H⁺ on the left and one H₂O on the right.
common_mistakes: Cancelling every H⁺ or every H₂O. Exactly 2H⁺ and 1H₂O survive.
Multiplying the dichromate half by 3 as well.
steps.memory_tip: 14 minus 12 leaves 2H⁺; 7 minus 6 leaves one water. Small leftover terms are normal in these additions.
steps.margin_note: The boxed equation with the atom and charge check earns this mark.

insider_note: Asked in March 2009 alongside the permanganate variant. The examiner looks first at the electron cancellation line and the remaining 2H⁺ — both must be visible, not implied.
